country_overview: The United States Federal Reserve System (the Federal Reserve) is the central bank and sets monetary policy, while U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) administer cross-border currency reporting. The United States operates one of the most liberalised foreign-exchange regimes in the world: there are no general exchange controls and no restrictions on current or capital account transactions for residents or non-residents. The US dollar is the world's primary reserve currency.

summary.traveler: Travelers may carry unlimited US dollars or foreign currency, but any person transporting more than USD 10,000 in aggregate — cash or monetary instruments — into or out of the United States must file a Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) with CBP at the border. Amounts of USD 10,000 or less require no declaration.
summary.business: Businesses and individuals enjoy full freedom to hold, transfer, convert and repatriate foreign currency through authorised banks and financial institutions.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency and US dollars may be imported without limit or prohibition. Any person bringing more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) into the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with a CBP officer at the port of entry.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: US dollars and foreign currency may be exported without limit. Any person taking more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) out of the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with CBP before departure; non-residents may freely re-export funds they lawfully brought in.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The reporting threshold is USD 10,000. Under 31 U.S.C. 5316 and 31 CFR 1010.340, transporting an aggregate amount exceeding that figure across the US border triggers a mandatory Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) to CBP. This traveler border report is distinct from Bank Secrecy Act filings by financial institutions — Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — and from Foreign Bank Account Reports (FBAR); none of those is a traveler declaration.
rules.resident_holding_rules: US residents may hold and maintain foreign currency accounts freely with authorised banks and financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may open and operate foreign currency accounts and transfer funds freely without prior approval.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in foreign currency or USD. Cross-border payments and repatriation of funds are handled freely through authorised financial institutions.
rules.exchange_controls: The United States maintains no general exchange controls. The regime is fully liberalised for both current and capital account transactions.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign exchange conversion and transfers are widely available through banks, licensed money exchange houses, and ATMs throughout the United States.
